13700:
A requisition is a formal, official request — usually written — made to obtain something that is needed. But it's not just any ordinary request. What makes a requisition special is that it carries authority and weight behind it. It typically happens within an organization, institution, or government system, and it follows an established, recognized process.

Think of it this way: when you ask a friend to lend you a pen, that's just a request. But when a hospital manager fills out an official form to obtain 200 syringes from the medical supply department, that is a requisition. The difference is formality, authority, and process.
The Two Main Things a "Requisition" Can Mean

1. The Act of Formally Requesting Something

A requisition refers to the official act of asking for something — particularly goods, materials, equipment, or services — through a proper, authorized channel. This is extremely common in workplaces, the military, and government.

For example:

  • A soldier's unit puts in a requisition for more fuel and ammunition before a mission.
  • A school principal submits a requisition for 30 new textbooks.
  • An office manager files a requisition for a new printer.

In all these cases, the person isn't just casually asking. They are going through an official system to formally request what they need, often because they have the recognized authority or need to justify and document the request.

2. The Written Document Itself

A requisition is also the name of the actual physical or digital form/document used to make such a request. So the word refers both to the action and the paperwork involved.

For example:

  • "Please fill out a requisition before taking any equipment from the storeroom."
  • "The manager approved the requisition and sent it to the procurement department."

Here, the requisition is the form you fill out. It typically includes details like what you need, how many, why you need it, who is requesting it, and the date.
The Deeper Shade of Meaning: Authority and the Right to Demand

Here is where requisition becomes a richer word than simple "request." In more serious or powerful contexts — especially military, wartime, or governmental — a requisition is not merely asking. It is a formal, authoritative demand, sometimes backed by legal power, where the requesting party essentially has the right to take or use what they are claiming.

For example:

  • During a war, a government might issue a requisition for private citizens' vehicles or land to support the military effort. This isn't a polite ask — it is an official claim with authority. The citizens are expected to comply.
  • A court might issue a requisition for certain documents to be handed over.

So in these contexts, the word carries a sense of compulsion — the person or authority making the requisition doesn't just want something, they are formally asserting their right to have it.

You may occasionally come across the phrase "in requisition," which means something is in great demand or constantly being called upon and used.

For example:

  • "The community hall was in constant requisition during the festival season."

This just means the hall was being requested and used all the time. This usage is less common today but worth knowing.

No matter the context, a requisition always involves these core elements:

Formality — it's not casual or verbal; it follows a procedure.
Authority — it comes from or is directed to someone with recognized power or responsibility.
A clear need — it exists to obtain something specific: goods, services, materials, property, or information.
Documentation — it is typically recorded, written, or filed.
How Requisition Differs from Similar Words

Request is the broadest and most casual word. Anyone can make a request at any time with no special process. A requisition is a specific kind of request — more formal, more official, and more structured.

Order implies the transaction is already decided and is being commanded. A requisition is still a formal asking, even if it carries authority.

Demand sounds aggressive or forceful in everyday language. A requisition is also firm and authoritative, but it works within a system — it's procedural and dignified rather than confrontational.

Application is a formal request too, but usually made by an outsider (like applying for a job or a permit). A requisition is typically made within a system — by someone who already belongs to the organization or has established authority.
Everyday Examples to Cement the Idea

• A nurse fills out a requisition for extra medical gloves from the hospital's supply room.
  • A field commander submits a requisition for helicopter support.
  • A teacher sends in a requisition for art supplies for the upcoming semester.
  • A wartime government issues a requisition for all privately owned radio equipment in the country.
  • An IT department receives a requisition for 10 new laptops from the marketing team.

In short, a requisition is an official, formal request — and sometimes a formal demand — made through a recognized process, usually documented in writing, most commonly seen in organizational, military, and governmental settings. It is the word that sits right at the border between asking and officially claiming, depending on how much authority is behind it.
13701:
Requital means giving back something in return for what someone has done to you. Think of it as the act of balancing the scales — if someone does something for you (or to you), and you respond by giving them something back in return, that response is the requital.

The key thing to understand is that requital works in both directions — it can be a repayment of something good, or a repayment of something bad. This is what makes it a rich and precise word.

When someone shows you love, kindness, loyalty, or a good deed, and you respond by giving the same back, that is a requital of their goodness. For example, if a friend stood by you during the hardest years of your life and you later devoted yourself to caring for them in their old age, your devotion is a requital of their friendship. You are returning what was given to you.

This positive meaning often carries a sense of warmth and moral fairness — a sense that goodness deserves to be answered with goodness.

Requital equally applies when the original act was harmful. If someone betrays you, hurts you, or wrongs you, and you respond by making them feel the consequences of that — whether through punishment, revenge, or justice — that too is requital. A person who was cheated by a business partner and later exposes them publicly has enacted a requital of the wrong done to them.

In this darker sense, requital is close in feeling to revenge or retribution, but it is a calmer, more neutral word. It simply means the return of harm for harm, without necessarily judging whether that return was righteous or excessive.

What unites both sides — the kind requital and the harsh requital — is this: requital is always a response, never a first action. It is always triggered by something that came before it. Something happens first, and requital is what follows as a deliberate return. Without that original act, there is no requital. This is what separates it from random acts of kindness or random cruelty — requital is always answering something.

Requital is a formal, literary word. You will not hear it in casual conversation — you are far more likely to encounter it in classic literature, poetry, formal writing, or speeches. In everyday speech, people would say "payback," "repayment," "revenge," or "returning the favor" depending on the situation. Requital covers all of these, but with a more dignified and serious tone.
How it differs from similar words

Retaliation is only negative — it always means striking back against harm. Requital can be positive or negative.

Gratitude is the feeling of thankfulness. Requital is the action of paying that thankfulness back. You can feel gratitude without offering requital; requital is when you actually do something about it.

Reward is something given by a person in a position of authority or advantage. Requital is more personal and mutual — it is about you responding to what was done specifically to you.

Compensation is usually about money or practical redress. Requital can be emotional, moral, or relational — it is far broader.

You will often see requital used in the phrase "in requital of" something. This simply means "as a return for" or "in response to." For example: "She gave her life in requital of the sacrifice he had made for her" means she gave her life because of and in response to his sacrifice — as a way of honoring and repaying it.

"He asked for no requital — he had helped her simply because it was right."
(He wanted nothing back in return for his help.)

"The destruction of his village was a requital for years of oppression that his people had suffered."
(The destruction was their answer — their payback — for what had been done to them.)

"She showered him with kindness in requital of his loyalty during her darkest years."
(She gave him kindness back because of the loyalty he had shown her.)
The single sentence that captures everything

If you ever need to recall this word quickly, remember this: requital is the act of giving back — whether good for good, or harm for harm — in response to what someone has done to you. It is the completion of a moral or emotional circle.
13702:
To requite something means to return a feeling, action, or treatment that someone gave you first. It's about giving back — matching what you received.

Think of it as completing a circle. Someone starts the circle by doing something to you or feeling something for you. When you requite it, you complete that circle by giving something back in return.

The word works in both positive and negative situations.

Positive — returning love, kindness, or a good deed:

When someone loves you and you love them back, you requite their love. When someone shows you loyalty and you are loyal to them in return, you requite their loyalty.

"He had loved her for years, and she finally requited his feelings."
(= She finally loved him back.)

"She requited every act of kindness he had shown her."
(= She paid back his kindness with kindness of her own.)

Negative — returning harm, betrayal, or cruelty:

You can also requite something bad — a wrong done to you, an insult, or a betrayal. In this sense, it means to pay someone back for the harm they caused, similar to retaliation or revenge.

"He requited their treachery by cutting all ties with them."
(= He paid them back for their betrayal.)

"She requited his cruelty with cold indifference."
(= She responded to his cruelty with deliberate coldness.)
The Key Ingredient: It Must Be Intentional

Requiting is always a deliberate, conscious act. You choose to return what you received. It's never accidental. There's a sense of fairness or balance behind it — making things even, whether through returned affection or returned punishment.

The word you will most commonly encounter in real life is unrequited — the negative form, meaning "not returned."

Unrequited love is love that one person feels strongly but the other person does not return. The circle never gets completed.

"His love was unrequited — she simply did not feel the same way."

So if you ever see or hear "unrequited," now you know it literally means: the requiting (the returning) never happened.

You can requite a person or a thing:

  • Requite a person → you are paying them back (for something they did)
    • "She requited him for his generosity." (She paid him back for being generous.)
  • Requite a feeling or action → you are returning that specific thing
    • "He never requited her affection." (He never returned her affection.)
The Register: When and Where Is This Word Used?

Requite is a formal, literary word. You would not hear it in casual everyday speech. It lives in literature, poetry, formal writing, and careful, educated conversation. If you said "I will requite your kindness" in a conversation, it would sound elevated and poetic, not odd — but definitely not casual.

The adjective form unrequited is far more common in everyday use than the verb itself, almost always paired with love, feelings, or affection.
To requite means to return — deliberately and in full — a feeling, action, or treatment that someone gave you first, whether that return is warm (love, kindness) or cold (revenge, punishment).
13703:
To rescind something means to officially cancel, withdraw, or take back a decision, agreement, law, or order that was previously made — as if it never existed or as if it no longer holds any power.

Think of it this way: when you rescind something, you are undoing an official act. You put something into place, and now you are pulling it back out.
The Key Idea: It Has to Be Something "Official"

This is the most important thing to understand about "rescind." You don't rescind casual, everyday things. You rescind things that carry formal authority or weight — things like:

  • A law or regulation
  • A job offer
  • A contract
  • A policy
  • An order or decree
  • A decision made by a committee, court, or organization
  • A membership or license

So if you told your friend you'd meet them for lunch and then changed your mind, you wouldn't say you rescinded your plan. But if a company sent you a formal job offer letter and then officially withdrew it, they rescinded the offer.

• The government rescinded the law after massive public protests. (The law was cancelled.)
  • The university rescinded her admission after discovering she had lied on her application. (The admission was officially taken back.)
  • The board rescinded its earlier decision and voted again. (They cancelled their previous decision.)
  • After the scandal, his security clearance was rescinded. (It was officially revoked.)

When something is rescinded, it stops being valid or enforceable. The act of rescinding doesn't just pause or freeze something — it eliminates its power and effect. In legal and formal settings especially, rescinding something often means treating it as though it should no longer be recognized or acted upon going forward.

Imagine a government passes a rule. That rule has power — people must follow it. The moment the government rescinds that rule, it loses its power. Done. Gone.

Rescinding often carries a sense of reversal and sometimes consequence. It's not a light or casual action. When something is rescinded, it usually means:

  • Something went wrong (e.g., fraud, a mistake, new circumstances), or
  • Someone in power deliberately changed course, or
  • A situation changed so significantly that the original decision no longer makes sense

So there's usually a reason behind a rescission, and it often affects people in significant ways (you lose a job offer, a law stops applying, a contract dissolves).
How It Differs from Similar Words

Since you want to know this word deeply, it helps to understand how it sits among similar words:

  • Cancel is the broad, everyday word. You can cancel a pizza order, a meeting, a show. Rescind is more formal and specific to official acts.
  • Revoke is very close in meaning and often interchangeable with rescind. However, revoke tends to be used when taking back a privilege or right given to a person (a driver's license is revoked, a permit is revoked). Rescind is broader and more commonly used for decisions, laws, orders, and contracts.
  • Repeal is specifically used for laws and legislation. A law is repealed through a legislative process. While you can also say a law is rescinded, repeal is the more precise legal term for that narrow case.
  • Annul typically means to declare something legally void from the beginning — as though it never existed (commonly used for marriages or contracts). Rescind is similar but doesn't always imply it was invalid from the start — it just means it is being cancelled now.
  • Withdraw is softer and more general. You withdraw an offer in a casual or early-stage sense. Rescind is the formal, official version of withdrawal.

In real life, you'll most often see "rescind" paired with these words:

  • Rescind an offer (especially a job offer)
  • Rescind a contract
  • Rescind a law or policy
  • Rescind an order (executive order, court order)
  • Rescind a decision
  • Rescind approval or authorization
  • Rescind membership or accreditation

To rescind = to officially cancel or take back a formal decision, agreement, or rule, stripping it of its power or validity.

If you remember that one line and the idea that it always involves something official, you'll use and understand this word correctly every single time.
13704:
Rescission is the act of officially canceling, wiping out, or undoing an agreement, contract, or law — in such a way that it is treated as though it never existed in the first place.

That phrase — "never existed in the first place" — is the absolute heart of this word. Rescission doesn't simply end something and move on. It erases the thing going backward in time, restoring everyone involved to the exact position they were in before the agreement ever happened.
The Big Idea: Turning Back the Clock

Think of it this way. Imagine you and a friend make a deal. You give him your bike, and he gives you $200. Later, you discover he lied to you to make the deal happen. A regular cancellation would say, "The deal is over — you keep your money and I keep my bike." But rescission goes further and says: "This deal is being erased. It never legally happened. Give me my bike back, and I'll give you your $200 back. We are back to square one."

This "return to square one" quality is what makes rescission different from almost every other word that involves ending or canceling something. It is retroactive — meaning it acts backward, not just forward.

Rescission is most commonly used in three areas:

1. Contract Law (the most common use)

In everyday legal life, rescission is used to completely undo a contract. When a contract is rescinded, it is voided from the very beginning — lawyers call this void ab initio, meaning "void from the start." Any goods exchanged must be returned, any money paid must be refunded, and any work done may need to be compensated, so that no one is left worse off than before the contract existed.

2. Real Estate

Rescission is especially important in property transactions. In many countries, when you sign a contract to buy a home, you are legally given a short window of time — often called a "rescission period" or "cooling-off period" — during which you can change your mind, cancel the purchase contract, and get your deposit back. The contract is treated as though it was never signed. This protects buyers from making rushed decisions on one of the biggest purchases of their lives.

3. Laws and Government Orders

Rescission is also used when a government, court, or authority formally cancels a law, regulation, order, or decision. For example, a government might pass a rescission of a previous policy, meaning that policy is officially withdrawn and no longer has any force — as if it were struck off the books.

A contract or agreement is not rescinded randomly. There must be a valid legal reason. The most recognized reasons include:

Fraud — One party deliberately lied or deceived the other to get them to sign. If you buy a car and the seller secretly knew the engine was broken and lied about it, that is fraud, and you may be entitled to rescission.

Misrepresentation — Similar to fraud, but the false statement may have been made without intent to deceive. Even an honest but incorrect statement that caused you to enter a contract can be grounds for rescission.

Mistake — Both parties were operating under a fundamental misunderstanding of the key facts at the time the contract was made. If both a buyer and seller believed a painting was an original masterpiece but it turned out to be a forgery, and that belief was the entire reason the contract existed, rescission could apply.

Duress or Undue Influence — If someone was forced, threatened, or manipulated into signing an agreement, they did not give true free consent. Contracts entered under duress can be rescinded because genuine agreement never really existed.

Lack of Capacity — If a person was legally incapable of entering a contract at the time — for example, they were a minor, or mentally incapacitated — rescission can undo that agreement.

Failure of Consideration — "Consideration" in contract law means what each party gives in exchange (money, goods, services, a promise). If one party completely fails to deliver what they promised, the other party may be able to seek rescission.
Rescission vs. Termination: A Crucial Distinction

These two words are often confused, so it is worth making the difference crystal clear.

Termination ends a contract going forward from a certain point. Everything that happened before termination remains legally valid. If you hired someone for a year, paid them for six months, and then terminated the contract, those six months of payments and work stand — the contract just stops now.

Rescission goes further and says the contract was defective from birth. It is not just ended; it is annulled. It is as if it was never formed. The goal is to undo everything, returning all parties to their original positions. This is why courts take rescission very seriously — it is a much more powerful and complete remedy than simple termination.

A helpful way to remember this: termination is like closing a book at chapter six. Rescission is like shredding the book and pretending it was never written.

Mutual Rescission happens when both parties to a contract voluntarily and jointly agree to cancel it. They both want out. In this case, they simply agree that the contract is over and work out how to return things to the way they were. This is the most peaceful and straightforward form of rescission.

Unilateral Rescission is when only one party wants to cancel the contract, and they do so on legal grounds (such as fraud or misrepresentation). The other party may or may not agree. In these cases, the matter often ends up before a court, which then decides whether rescission is legally warranted.

Rescission can be granted in two ways:

By agreement between the parties (mutual rescission, as described above), without needing a court.

By a court or legal authority, when one party applies for rescission and the court rules in their favor based on legal grounds like fraud or duress.

Once rescission is granted or agreed upon, the legal doctrine of restitution kicks in. Restitution means restoring each party to their original position. Money is refunded. Property is returned. Any unjust enrichment — meaning any benefit one party unfairly gained from the other through the flawed contract — must be given back. The law tries to make it as though the contract simply never happened.
A Quick Real-World Example to Tie It All Together

You sign a contract to buy a piece of land for $50,000. You pay the money and the deal closes. Later, you discover that the seller had a legal obligation to tell you the land was contaminated, and they deliberately hid this from you — that is fraud.

You go to court and seek rescission of the contract. The court agrees. The contract is declared void from the very beginning. The seller must give you back your $50,000. You must give back the land. Neither party profits from the fraudulent deal. You are both, as closely as possible, returned to where you stood before any of it happened.

That entire process — the legal undoing of that contract from its root — is rescission.
Rescission is the complete legal cancellation of a contract, law, or agreement that wipes it out as if it never existed, restoring all parties to their original position before it was made.
13705:
A rescript is an official written reply issued by a supreme authority — such as a ruler, emperor, or the Pope — in direct response to a formal question, petition, or legal inquiry submitted to them. Think of it as a very powerful, formal written answer that carries the weight of law or binding authority.

The word is not used in casual everyday life. It belongs to the worlds of law, history, government, and religious administration.

Imagine you are living under an emperor's rule, and you have a legal dispute you can't resolve. Ordinary courts are stumped. So you write a formal petition directly to the emperor asking: "Your Majesty, what is the law in this situation?" The emperor reviews your case and writes back an official answer. That written answer — authoritative, formal, and binding — is a rescript.

The key things that make something a rescript are:

  • It comes from the highest authority (an emperor, a pope, a sovereign power).
  • It is a response — it only exists because someone first asked a question or submitted a petition.
  • It is written and official.
  • It carries binding or legal force, meaning it isn't just an opinion. It settles the matter.
The Two Main Contexts Where You'll Encounter This Word

1. Roman Law and Imperial Rescripts

This is the most historically important use of the word. In ancient Rome, one of the primary ways Roman emperors created law was through rescripts. Judges, governors, magistrates, and even private citizens could write to the emperor asking for a legal ruling on a specific situation. The emperor — or his legal advisors writing in his name — would study the question and issue a formal written reply.

This reply, the rescript, was then treated as the authoritative interpretation of the law for that case, and often served as a legal precedent that guided future cases as well. Hundreds of these imperial rescripts were collected and preserved in great Roman legal compilations, like the Codex of Justinian, where they helped form the backbone of Roman law as we know it today.

So in this context, a rescript is both an act of governance and an act of lawmaking — the emperor speaking with full legal authority in writing.

2. The Catholic Church and Papal Rescripts

The second major context is the Catholic Church, which inherited much of its administrative structure from Roman traditions. Here, a rescript is an official written document issued by the Pope or another competent Church authority (such as a Vatican office) in response to a formal request or petition submitted by a person, a group, or even a bishop.

Rescripts in this context are used to:

  • Grant a dispensation (an exception from a Church rule or law for a specific person or situation, e.g., allowing a marriage that would normally be restricted by canon law).
  • Grant a privilege or special permission.
  • Provide an authoritative answer to a question of Church law or doctrine.

A rescript from the Pope does not just express a wish — it formally grants or decides something. It has legal standing within canon law (the internal law of the Catholic Church). Once issued, it creates a real, binding change in the legal situation of the person who petitioned for it.
An Analogy to Make It Click

Think of a rescript like a formal written ruling from a judge, but the "judge" here is the single most powerful authority in that world — the emperor of an empire or the head of the Church — and the ruling only came into being because someone first asked for it. It's the highest possible written response to a formal question, and it carries the force of law.

Contrast this with a decree or edict, which is issued on the authority's own initiative to address the general public. A rescript is reactive and specific — it answers a question directed at the authority.

It is always a response. This is fundamental. A rescript cannot exist without a prior petition or inquiry. If the authority issues something on their own initiative, that is a different kind of document (like an edict or decree). The reactive, responsive nature of a rescript is what defines it.

It is specific, not general. Rescripts typically address the specific question or situation raised by the petitioner. While they can be used as precedent, they are not inherently meant to be broad laws for everyone.

It can be misused. Historically, people sometimes obtained rescripts by providing false information in their petition. Roman and Church law both recognized this problem. A rescript obtained through deceit or misrepresentation was considered invalid — the authority's reply was only binding if it was based on accurate information.

The word can be used more loosely. In some literary or historical contexts, "rescript" is used more broadly to mean any kind of official restatement, revised directive, or formal written response from a government authority — not necessarily from the very top. But when used precisely, it refers to the specific Roman/legal/canonical tradition described above.

A rescript is a formal, authoritative, written response issued by a supreme power — classically a Roman emperor or the Pope — to a specific question or petition directed at them. It has the force of law or binding authority within its domain. It is defined by three things: it comes from the top, it responds to a specific request, and it is written. You'll encounter this word most often in discussions of Roman law, legal history, and Catholic canon law.
13706:
Research is a careful, organized effort to find out the truth about something — or to discover new knowledge about it — by collecting information, studying it, and drawing conclusions from it.

The key word here is careful. Research is not just typing a quick question into Google and reading the first result. It is a deliberate, methodical process where someone sets out to answer a specific question or solve a specific problem, and does so by gathering reliable evidence.

Think of it this way: if you wonder whether eating sugar before bed affects sleep, and you just ask a friend, that's curiosity. But if you read scientific studies, look at data from experiments, compare findings from multiple sources, and form a conclusion based on all that — that is research.

Research has a few defining qualities:

  • It has a purpose. There is always a specific question being investigated or a gap in knowledge being filled.
  • It is systematic. It follows a plan or method, not random guessing.
  • It relies on evidence. Conclusions come from data, observation, experiments, documents, or other verifiable sources — not just personal opinion.
  • It aims for accuracy. The goal is to find what is actually true, not just what seems convenient or easy.

Research does not look the same in every field. It takes different shapes depending on what is being investigated:

Scientific research involves experiments and observations. A scientist studying a new drug, for example, runs controlled trials, measures results, and analyzes the data before drawing any conclusion.

Academic research is done by scholars and students. It involves reading existing work on a topic (called a "literature review"), identifying what is still unknown, and then contributing new understanding through study or analysis.

Market research is done by businesses to understand their customers — what people want, what they buy, what they think of a product. This often involves surveys, interviews, and sales data.

Historical research involves studying old documents, records, letters, and artifacts to understand the past.

Investigative research is what journalists do — digging into facts, sources, and records to report the truth about an event or situation.

All of these are "research," but they look very different in practice. What they share is that same core: a disciplined search for reliable, accurate knowledge.

This is an important distinction:

Primary research means going directly to the source. You collect new data yourself — through experiments, surveys, interviews, or direct observation. The knowledge doesn't exist yet in a collected form; you are the one creating it.

Secondary research means working with information that already exists. You read books, articles, reports, and studies that others have produced, and you analyze or synthesize that information. Most students and professionals do a great deal of secondary research.

Both are genuinely called "research." Neither is better than the other — the right type depends on the question being asked.

You will often hear these two terms when research is discussed:

Quantitative research deals with numbers and measurable data. How many? How much? By what percentage? It answers questions through statistics and figures. Example: a study showing that 68% of teenagers sleep less than 8 hours a night.

Qualitative research deals with meaning, experience, and description — things that can't easily be reduced to numbers. Why do teenagers sleep less? What does that feel like? How do they describe their habits? This type of research uses interviews, observations, and open-ended conversations.

Both are valid, and many research projects combine the two.
Research as a Body of Knowledge

"Research" as a noun can refer not just to the process of investigating, but also to the result of that process — the collected findings and conclusions themselves.

So when someone says "the research shows that exercise improves memory," they are referring to the accumulated body of studies and findings that have been produced on that topic. The word here points to the product — the knowledge that the process of researching has generated.

This is an important dual meaning to understand:

  • "She is conducting research" — here, research refers to the activity (the process of investigating).
  • "The research is clear on this matter" — here, research refers to the body of evidence (the conclusions that have been established).

Understanding what research is becomes sharper when you understand what it is not:

  • Casual reading is not research. Skimming an article for general interest is not research; systematically reviewing sources to answer a specific question is.
  • Opinion is not research. Someone's personal belief, however strongly held, is not research. Research requires evidence.
  • Hearsay is not research. What someone heard someone else say is not research. Research traces claims back to their original, verifiable sources.
  • A single source is usually not enough for strong research. Good research draws on multiple, independent, reliable sources to verify that a finding holds up.

Research is how humanity moves forward. Almost everything we know about medicine, technology, psychology, economics, history, and the natural world comes from research. It is the tool we use to separate fact from assumption, to test ideas against reality, and to build knowledge that is reliable enough to act on.

When a doctor decides how to treat an illness, they rely on medical research. When a government makes a policy decision, it should rely on economic and social research. When a company launches a product, it relies on market research. Research, in this sense, is the foundation on which informed decisions are made.

Here are examples showing the range of ways "research" functions as a noun:

  • "His research on climate change took five years to complete." (the process of investigating)
  • "The research suggests a strong link between stress and heart disease." (the body of findings)
  • "She published her research in a scientific journal." (the documented results of an investigation)
  • "More research is needed before we can be certain." (further investigation is required)
  • "This is based on solid research, not guesswork." (evidence-backed knowledge, contrasted with opinion)

Research, as a noun, is the careful, organized investigation of a subject — using reliable evidence — with the goal of discovering truth, answering a question, or generating new knowledge. It can refer both to the process of doing that investigation and to the body of knowledge that results from it. It is systematic, evidence-based, and purposeful, and it is the primary way humans have come to understand the world around them with any real confidence.
13707:
A resemblance is the quality of looking alike or being similar to someone or something else. When two things share noticeable common features — in the way they look, sound, feel, or behave — there is a resemblance between them.

The word captures the fact that two things are not the same thing, but they are similar enough that you notice the connection.

Resemblance is most naturally used for visible, outward similarity — things you can see or perceive directly. The most classic example is a family resemblance: a child who has the same nose or eyes as a parent. You look at both people, notice the shared feature, and say there is a resemblance.

But resemblance isn't limited to physical appearance. It can describe similarity in:

  • Sound — a song that resembles another song
  • Character or personality — a shy person whose behaviour resembles that of their quiet parent
  • Style or manner — a painting that bears resemblance to the works of a famous artist
  • Structure or form — an idea that shows resemblance to an older theory

The common thread is always: two things share enough features that the similarity is noticeable.

One of the most important things to understand about resemblance is that it comes in degrees. It is not an all-or-nothing word. Two things can share a little resemblance or a lot.

This is why you will almost always see resemblance paired with a describing word:

  • A striking/close/strong resemblance — the similarity is very obvious and hard to miss. If someone says a boy bears a striking resemblance to his grandfather, it means you can immediately see how alike they look.
  • A faint/slight/vague resemblance — the similarity is there, but it is weak and easy to miss. You might need to look carefully.
  • A passing resemblance — a very loose, superficial similarity. The two things are not really much alike, but there is just enough of a shared quality to mention it. ("She bears a passing resemblance to a celebrity" — meaning they look a little alike, but not strongly.)
  • An uncanny resemblance — a resemblance that is so surprisingly strong that it feels almost eerie or unnatural. ("The twins had an uncanny resemblance to each other even though they were raised in different countries.")
How It Is Used in Sentences

The most natural and common structure is: to bear a resemblance to something or someone.

"The new building bears a striking resemblance to the old town hall."

"He bears no resemblance to his father at all."

"There is a close resemblance between the two paintings."

"I can see a family resemblance — you and your sister have the same smile."

"The proposal bears a resemblance to a plan we rejected last year."

"Despite the superficial resemblance, the two concepts are fundamentally different."

Notice that you bear a resemblance, or there is a resemblance — you don't usually "have" a resemblance. This is just how the word naturally fits into English sentences.
The Idea of Resemblance vs. Being Identical

This distinction is built into the very meaning of the word. Resemblance acknowledges similarity, not sameness.

If two things were completely identical — exact copies — you wouldn't say they "resemble" each other. You would just say they are the same. Resemblance always implies that the two things are separate, and despite being different things, they share enough in common that the likeness is worth pointing out.

This is why the word is useful. It lets you say: "These two things are different, but look at how similar they are."
A Few More Examples Across Different Contexts

People:

"The detective noticed a resemblance between the suspect's handwriting and the ransom note."

"She was startled by her own resemblance to her grandmother in the old photograph."

Things and places:

"The flavour of the fruit has a resemblance to mango, though it is much more tart."

"The town bore a resemblance to the small villages of southern France."

Ideas and concepts:

"His philosophy shows a resemblance to the teachings of the Stoics."

"The two films have a certain resemblance in their themes of loss and redemption."
Related Words in the Same Family

Understanding the whole word family makes the meaning stick better:

  • Resemble (verb) — the action form. "She resembles her aunt." To resemble something is to look or be like it.
  • Resemblance (noun) — the state or quality of resembling. "There is a resemblance between them."
  • Resembling (adjective/participle) — describing something in the act of being like something else. "A structure resembling a bridge."

These two words are very close in meaning, and in many sentences you can swap them. But there is a subtle difference:

Similarity is broader. It can describe any kind of likeness — in function, in purpose, in structure, in results.

Resemblance leans more toward perceptible, observable likeness — the kind you can see, hear, or directly notice. It feels more concrete and sensory.

"There is a similarity between how the two machines work." (function)

"There is a resemblance between how the two machines look." (appearance — more natural here)

Both are correct in many cases, but if you want to emphasise how something looks or how it is perceived, resemblance is the stronger, more precise choice.

Resemblance means: the observable quality of being similar to something or someone else. It lives in the space between "completely different" and "exactly the same." When you notice that two things share common features — especially in how they appear — that shared quality is their resemblance.

The stronger the common features, the stronger the resemblance. The weaker the common features, the fainter the resemblance. And when two things share no features worth noticing, there is no resemblance at all.
13708:
To resemble something or someone means to be similar to them — to share noticeable characteristics with them. Those characteristics can be in appearance, behavior, personality, structure, sound, smell, or any other quality.

The simplest way to understand it: if A resembles B, then looking at or experiencing A reminds you of B, because they share something in common.

"She resembles her mother." → She looks like her mother / they look similar.
"This fruit resembles an apple." → This fruit looks like an apple; they share similar features.

Resemblance is not about being identical. It is about being similar enough that the likeness is noticeable. Two things can resemble each other while still being quite different overall. The similarity is real but partial.

Think of it like an overlap in a Venn diagram — the two things share some traits, but not everything.

"The new building resembles the old one." → They are not the same building, but they have things in common — maybe the shape, the color, the style.
What kinds of similarity does "resemble" cover?

"Resemble" is wide in its reach. It is not limited only to how things look. It can describe similarity in:

  • Appearance — the most common use
    "He resembles a young Al Pacino."
  • Behavior or personality
    "Her stubbornness resembles her grandfather's."
  • Structure or organization
    "This system resembles the one used in Germany."
  • Sound
    "This word resembles the word 'desert' in pronunciation."
  • Feel, quality, or character
    "The situation resembles a chess game — every move matters."

1. "Resemble" always needs an object.
You always resemble something or someone. The verb cannot stand alone.

✅ "This cloud resembles a dragon."
❌ "This cloud resembles." ← Incomplete; resembles what?

2. "Resemble" is never used in the continuous (–ing) form.
This is one of the most common mistakes learners make.

❌ "She is resembling her mother."
✅ "She resembles her mother."

This is because "resemble" is a stative verb — it describes a state or condition that simply exists, not an action happening at a moment. Other stative verbs like "know," "own," and "believe" follow the same rule. You would never say "I am knowing the answer." Similarly, you never say "He is resembling his father."

3. It is used in both past and present tense normally.

Present: "The twins resemble each other closely."
Past: "The ruins resembled a forgotten city."
Perfect: "No one has ever resembled him as much as his son does."
How to describe the degree of resemblance

One of the most useful things to know: you can modify "resemble" with adverbs to say how much or how strongly something resembles something else.

Strong resemblance:

  • closely, strongly, remarkably, strikingly, uncannily

"He closely resembles the actor."
"She remarkably resembles her great-grandmother."
"The two designs are uncannily similar." ← notice "resemble" can be replaced here too

Weak resemblance:

  • slightly, barely, faintly, vaguely, loosely, superficially

"This plan only vaguely resembles what we discussed."
"The two brothers barely resemble each other."
"It faintly resembles a smile."

Understanding how "resemble" compares to related expressions will sharpen your understanding:

"Look like" — casual, mostly about visual appearance

"He looks like his dad." ← natural in everyday speech
"He resembles his dad." ← slightly more formal; also covers non-visual traits

Both are correct when talking about appearance. "Resemble" just tends to feel a touch more formal and can stretch into non-visual territory more naturally.

"Take after" — specifically about resembling a parent or ancestor, either in looks or personality

"She takes after her mother — same eyes, same temper."

"Take after" is narrower; it only works within families. "Resemble" works everywhere.

"Be similar to" — more abstract and general; works for ideas, objects, situations

"This situation is similar to what happened in 2008."

"Resemble" and "be similar to" often overlap, but "resemble" feels more vivid and direct, like you are pointing to a likeness you can perceive.

When you say A resembles B, it doesn't automatically mean B resembles A — at least not in terms of emphasis. The sentence is directional: you are saying A reminds you of B, or that you notice A through the lens of B.

"The student resembles the teacher." → You are comparing the student to the teacher.
"The teacher resembles the student." → Now the teacher is being compared to the student.

Both can be true at once, but which one you say depends on what you want to highlight.

"The child resembled neither of his parents."
"The new smartphone closely resembles last year's model."
"Her writing style resembles Hemingway's — short, direct sentences."
"Nothing about this town resembled what I had imagined."
"The two landscapes so strongly resembled each other that the travelers grew confused."
"He resembled a ghost — pale, silent, drifting from room to room."
To resemble means to be similar to something or someone in some noticeable way — whether in looks, behavior, structure, or character — without necessarily being identical to it.
13709:
To resent something or someone means to feel a lasting, bitter anger toward them because you believe they treated you unfairly, disrespectfully, or in a way you didn't deserve.

It's not just being annoyed. It's not just being upset in the moment. Resentment is the feeling that sits inside you — sometimes for days, months, or even years — because a wound hasn't healed.
What makes it different from ordinary anger

Regular anger can flare up and fade quickly. You stub your toe, you feel pain and frustration, and then it's gone. Resentment doesn't work that way.

When you resent someone, you hold onto the negative feeling. It smolders quietly. Every time you see that person, or every time something reminds you of what they did, that bitter feeling comes back. It's anger with memory.

Think of it this way: anger is a fire; resentment is the ash that stays warm long after the fire is out.

The key ingredient is a sense of injustice. You resent something when you feel:

  • You were treated unfairly
  • You were disrespected or humiliated
  • You were overlooked or not given what you deserved
  • Someone took advantage of you
  • You were forced to do something against your will
  • You were blamed for something that wasn't your fault

The feeling says: "This wasn't right. I didn't deserve this."

Importantly, you don't have to be objectively right for resentment to form. What matters is that you perceive the situation as unfair. Resentment is about how you feel, not necessarily about what actually happened.

• A student studies hard all semester but fails the exam while a classmate who barely studied passes. The student resents the teacher for what feels like unfair grading.
  • A woman has been working at a company for five years. A newcomer gets promoted over her without explanation. She resents her manager for the decision.
  • A child is always compared to their more successful sibling by their parents. As an adult, they still resent their parents for the way they were raised.
  • A man sacrifices his personal goals to support his family financially, but his family never acknowledges his efforts. He begins to resent them for taking him for granted.
  • A friend constantly cancels plans at the last minute. After many times, you resent them for not valuing your time.
What you can resent — the objects of resentment

Grammatically and in real life, you can resent:

A person:
"She resents her older brother."

An action or decision:
"He resents the fact that he was passed over for the promotion."

A situation or condition:
"They resent being treated like children at work."

Something someone said:
"She resented his comment about her appearance."

An experience:
"He resents every moment he spent in that toxic job."

Notice that you can even resent abstract things — a rule, a system, a circumstance — as long as you feel it wronged you in some way.
Grammar: how "resent" works in a sentence

The most important grammar pattern to know is that "resent" is very commonly followed by a gerund (a verb ending in -ing), not an infinitive.

✅ "I resent being ignored."
❌ "I resent to be ignored." ← This is wrong in English.

This is because "resent" refers to an experience that already happened or is ongoing — something you feel about an action — and gerunds are used for that in English.

Other patterns:

  • resent + noun/pronoun: "He resented her." / "She resented the decision."
  • resent + gerund: "I resent being treated unfairly."
  • resent + that-clause: "He resented that no one thanked him."
  • resent + possessive + gerund: "She resented his constant interrupting."

Resentment sits at a moderate-to-deep level of emotional intensity. It is:

  • Stronger than simple annoyance or irritation
  • Quieter and more internal than explosive rage
  • More specific than general dislike — it's tied to a particular wrong done to you
  • More personal than indifference — there's a wound underneath it

It's also worth noting that resentment often grows in relationships where there is some closeness or expectation. You tend to resent people who mattered to you, or whose opinion of you mattered. We rarely deeply resent strangers. We resent parents, friends, colleagues, bosses — people whose actions had real weight in our lives.
How to tell if someone "resents" rather than just "dislikes"

If someone simply dislikes a person, they just don't enjoy their company. But if someone resents a person, there's a story behind it — a specific thing that happened, a specific way they felt wronged. Resentment always has a reason, even if that reason is never spoken aloud.

A person might resent their father and still love him. A person might resent a close friend and still want their friendship. This is what makes resentment complex — it can exist alongside other emotions, and it doesn't necessarily mean you hate someone. It means a wound hasn't closed.
A one-line summary to anchor it all
To resent = to feel a lasting, bitter anger toward someone or something because you believe they treated you unfairly or in a way you didn't deserve.
